explanations.explanation: It’s a marker for sentence‐/segment–end punctuation (a “full stop” indicator) that triggers the model to switch into a mode appropriate for structured, formal or enumerated text—adjusting the next token prediction to match the conventional token (often a numeral, abbreviation, etc.) that follows a definitive period.

It appears that the feature signals an upcoming, purpose‐oriented or directive construction—essentially marking phrases (often with “to” or its equivalents) that lead into an intended action or next step in the discourse.

It appears the feature is “lighting up” on subword pieces that serve as the connective or completing morpheme of a multi‐token word. In other words, the high‐activation segments mark the internal “glue” or affix that signals the model should complete a compound or morphologically segmented word (as in “integrate” → “inte‐GR‐ate”, “procur a” → “cur”, “lot” in an informal phrase, etc.), whereas without it the continuation becomes a generic “row.”

It appears that this feature is “lighting‐up” when the language is asserting a defining or evaluative predicate—that is, when a sentence sets up a hallmark or benchmark statement (using words like “says,” “takes,” “aims,” “only,” “doesn’t,” etc.). In these contexts the model is selecting a verb or evaluative function word that frames the main claim, whereas without the feature it falls back to a generic “cept” (suggestive of “except”), indicating that the key evaluative element is missing.

This feature detects a canonical partitive construction—specifically the “one of the”–style phrase—that cues the model to expect a following determiner to complete a noun phrase expressing a part–whole relationship.

This feature activates when the model detects a sentence‐ or clause‐terminating punctuation mark (typically a period or similar delimiter) that signals the end of one thought and the beginning of another. In doing so it conditions the next-token prediction—ensuring that the following token fits a sentence‐initial context (e.g. proper capitalization and expected syntax)—whereas without the feature the model reverts to an anomalous, context–inappropriate continuation (e.g. “abad”).

It appears that the feature is a high‐level context or “discourse framing” signal that steers the model toward a coherent, domain‐appropriate continuation (e.g. proper names, event details, and location‐relevant vocabulary) rather than default, off‐context completions (like “burg” or “/”). In short, it marks that the text is in a particular informational or headline-like register and guides the next–token prediction accordingly.

It appears to be a feature that flags a sentence‐ (or clause-) closing punctuation context—a “boundary signal” that shifts the model’s next‐token distribution from a generic filler (defaulting to “er”) to one that’s contextually appropriate (like a new sentence’s proper start, number, or name).

It appears to be a feature that signals abbreviated or “closed‐class” periods—i.e. a period token that marks an abbreviation (such as month names, institutional abbreviations, or other shorthand) rather than serving as a sentence terminator, which in turn alters the predicted next token.

explanations.explanation: It’s a morpho‐completion signal that kicks in when the model sees an initial, capitalized or adjective/name fragment (like “Den–”, “Fab–”, “Ama–”, etc.), biasing the output toward a specific, well‐learned word ending (e.g. “ver”, “ol”, “prise”) rather than a more generic continuation.

It appears that this feature “lights up” when the model is in the midst of a fixed, highly conventional phrase or collocation—a syntactic‐collocational dependency signal. In such contexts (e.g. after “come”, “worked hard”, or a proper name like “Jeff”), the feature biases the model toward the specific, expected subsequent token (like “to”, “soon”, or “Sessions”), reflecting the learned routine continuation of common grammatical or formulaic expressions.
This feature is detecting sentence‐ or clause–final punctuation that signals the end of one coherent unit and triggers a change in context for the next token.

This feature appears to act as a trigger for producing specific, context‐appropriate modifier or compound elements (for example, in hyphenated fractions, numerical adjectives, or adverbials). In other words, it signals that the surrounding text is building a precise descriptive or quantitative phrase—and without it the model defaults to a generic continuation (like “well”).
This feature appears to detect the beginning of a negative contraction (like “don’t”), signaling the contraction’s split between its “don” piece and the following punctuation or morpheme.

It appears to be a detector for a sub‐word segment that “flags” that the model is in the middle of a proper‐name (or similar compound noun) construction. In other words, the feature fires when the token contains a typical affix or syllable found inside names (or name‐like words), which in turn shifts the model’s next‐token prediction toward a continuation of that name.

It’s a signal for sentence‐boundary punctuation—a feature that flags a terminal (typically “.”) token to mark the end of a sentence, thereby conditioning the following token’s distribution (e.g. starting a new sentence with a distinct style such as a numeral or proper noun).

It appears that this feature fires when the model is in a “sub‐word boundary” or “sticky token” context—that is, when a token is acting like an incomplete unit whose continuation is almost determined (often supplying a function word or a specific suffix fragment). In these examples the feature’s activation biases the next token prediction (e.g. “to”, “ol”, “ver”, etc.) so that it “completes” the morphemic or syntactic unit, whereas removing the feature shifts the prediction to a less coherent continuation.

It seems to be a “group‐reference” signal—that is, a feature that activates when the context is setting up a referent for a specific group or entity (using tokens like “their” or “those”) that will immediately be qualified or elaborated.

It seems that this feature “fires” when the language model is in the middle of a fixed, formula‐ or template–like phrase. In other words, it detects when the context is one of those conventional, boilerplate segments (whether in a URL’s query part, in legal or formal phrasing, or in standard “thank you for…” expressions) and thereby shifts the next–token distribution toward the expected continuation of that structure.

It appears that the feature is signaling a formal, announcement‐ or listing–style segment boundary—one where a strong punctuation (usually a period) marks the close of a structured “header” (often including dates, awards, event names, etc.) and cues that what comes next is a number or similarly formal element (such as a date or index). In other words, the feature encodes that the textual context is in a broadcast or official announcement format, and its presence shifts the next‐token distribution toward “structured” tokens (like a year or numeral) in that style.
